journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Accept, Adjust, or Move Forward: The Pivotal Additional Roles and Responsibilities of Black Teachers
text_snippet: Accept, Adjust, or Move Forward: The Pivotal Additional Roles and Responsibilities of Black Teachers This study explores the often unrecognized additional roles and responsibilities of Black teachers in K-12 education. Despite comprising only 7% of the teaching workforce, Black educators frequently assume duties beyond their formal job descriptions, including serving as mentors, cultural liaisons, disciplinarians, and advocates. Utilizing Role Theory, this research examines how these hidden roles impact Black teachers’ professional experiences, job satisfaction, and emotional well-being. Through semi-structured interviews with 17 Black teachers across various U.S. regions, the study reveals not only the burdens but also the sources of pride and fulfillment that these additional roles can generate. The findings highlight the urgent need for systemic changes, such as peer support groups, culturally relevant professional development, and equitable compensation policies. These measures aim to acknowledge and support the multifaceted contributions of Black teachers, ultimately fostering a more inclusive and sustainable educational environment.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: School Discipline: Assessing Cultural Misperception and Biased Perspective of Teachers
text_snippet: School Discipline: Assessing Cultural Misperception and Biased Perspective of Teachers School discipline aims to address problematic behaviors by suspending or removing disruptive students from class. Previous research indicates that school discipline negatively affects student outcomes, including reduced academic performance and heightened dropout rates (Anderson et al., 2019; Holt & Gershenson, 2019; Roch & Elsayed, 2020). Disparities remain stark, as minority students—particularly Black and Hispanic populations—are disproportionately suspended or expelled (Anderson & Ritter, 2020; Barrett et al., 2021; Nicholson-Crotty et al., 2009). Furthermore, these practices are more prevalent in schools serving students of color, those in high-poverty areas, and institutions with lower academic performance. This study investigates the factors on school discipline by analyzing data from the New York State Education Department (2007–2023). This research highlights the urgent need for equitable disciplinary practices that mitigate long-term adverse effects and address disparity in school discipline across school environments.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Building Motivation and Achievement in Urban Students: Insights From a Supportive Academy
text_snippet: Building Motivation and Achievement in Urban Students: Insights From a Supportive Academy This qualitative study explored what motivates urban students in an accelerated honors high school to learn. Forty-four students in grades 9-12 responded to a single, open-ended question: “What motivates you to learn?” Using grounded theory, the findings indicated that family was the primary motivator. Intrinsic motivation increased from grades 9-10 to 11-12, was higher among females, and was positively correlated with GPA.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Promoting a “Home for All” at an Urban Midwestern University Through a DEI Seminar Series
text_snippet: Promoting a “Home for All” at an Urban Midwestern University Through a DEI Seminar Series We explore changes in perceptions and actions related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) among faculty, staff, students, and community members who participated in a year-long seminar series at a university located in the urban core of a Midwestern city. The results of a pre-/post-survey to assess color-blind racial attitudes and post-project individual interviews demonstrate that participants changed their perceptions to adopt a broader definition of diversity and developed a new awareness of their own intersectional identities and biases. Participants also reflected on the cohort experience and relevance of the curriculum, and they engaged in actions in their professional and personal lives to apply concepts from the series. The paper shares implications for successful DEI professional development projects within urban higher education communities in an increasingly challenging political context.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Identifying the Depressive Subgroups Among Adolescent Black Boys and Adolescent White Boys Who Have Been School Policed and School Disciplined
text_snippet: Identifying the Depressive Subgroups Among Adolescent Black Boys and Adolescent White Boys Who Have Been School Policed and School Disciplined Objective: Identify and compare the nuances in depressive symptoms among adolescent Black boys and adolescent White Boys who experienced school policing and school discipline. Methods: Data from 1,099 adolescent boys (803 Black boys and 296 White boys) from the Future of Families & Child Wellbeing Study (FFCWS) were used to identify depressive subgroups among adolescent Black and White boys. I conducted a latent class analysis to examine the subgroup differences among respondents regarding school policing, school discipline, and depressive symptoms. The categorical indicators, school policing and school discipline, were measured by the following questions: “police officer or officers regularly stationed at school?”; “some other security guard regularly stationed at school?”; “stopped by police at school”; “ever seen someone stopped by police in your school?”; and “ever been suspended or expelled in the past two years?” The continuous indicator, depressive symptoms, was measured by using the CES-D 5. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Reimagining Academic Writing in Practice: Insights from Andragogical and Transformative Perspectives
text_snippet: Reimagining Academic Writing in Practice: Insights from Andragogical and Transformative Perspectives Academic writing conventions in higher education can create unintended barriers for adult learners who use diverse forms of English, often positioning their linguistic resources outside established scholarly norms. This article examines how andragogical and transformative learning principles can inform a more inclusive pedagogical framework for academic writing. Employing a critical autoethnographic methodology, the study draws upon the author’s lived experiences as a multilingual scholar and educator to analyze specific teaching practices. The analysis demonstrates that pedagogical approaches centered on translanguaging, asset-based feedback, and the cultivation of scholarly community effectively foster scholarly voice development and academic agency. This paper argues for a paradigmatic shift in writing pedagogy, from a deficit model focused on correction to an asset-based model that recognizes linguistic diversity as a catalyst for transformative learning. It concludes by offering a praxis-oriented framework to guide educators in creating equitable writing environments that empower varietal-English-speaking students and expand the possibilities of academic discourse.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Book Review- The Magnitude of Us: An Educator’s Guide to Creating Culturally Responsive Classrooms (2024)
text_snippet: Book Review- The Magnitude of Us: An Educator’s Guide to Creating Culturally Responsive Classrooms (2024) This review explores The Magnitude of Us: An Educator’s Guide to Creating Culturally Responsive Classrooms (2024) by Marlee S. Bunch, a detailed guide for educators committed to building inclusive and equitable learning environments. The content is centered around Bunch’s original un/HUSH framework, which stands for Uniting/Naming, Histories, Unlearning, Stories, and Healing. The book provides research-based strategies, reflective activities, and adaptable tools that support culturally responsive teaching. Each chapter offers multilingual content, helpful tips for preservice teachers, and opportunities for critical reflection, making it especially valuable for educators in training. The review recognizes the book’s strengths in accessibility, structure, and real-world application, while also noting areas for potential growth, such as addressing systemic barriers and engaging administrators and policymakers. Overall, this resource is highly recommended for educators, teacher educators, and stakeholders seeking to transform classroom practices and promote educational equity.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Interrogating professional identity: An analysis of preservice teachers’ racial identity development
text_snippet: Interrogating professional identity: An analysis of preservice teachers’ racial identity development The following qualitative study analyzed pre-service teachers’ reflective essays during an introductory place-based educational experience class. The analysis examined how racial identity is an integral component of preservice teachers’ professional identity development. Using Helm (2007) and Howard’s (2016) racial identity developmental model, student reflective essays demonstrated the complex and dynamic processes that preservice teachers experience when engaging in diverse place-based educational experiences.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Critical Disciplinary Literacy in Secondary Content Classrooms
text_snippet: Critical Disciplinary Literacy in Secondary Content Classrooms This study employed a qualitative, case study methodology to investigate how five urban secondary school teachers fostered student-centered learning communities within their classrooms. The primary focus was to comprehend how these teachers implemented critical disciplinary literacy (CDL) to enhance engagement and prioritize student needs in their teaching. Through the lens of CDL, the instructors sought to facilitate connections between students’ personal experiences, interests and voices within the curriculum; however, they also addressed broader societal issues. Data collection occurred through semi-structured interviews, during which teachers articulated their instructional strategies, beliefs and perceptions regarding their students. By analyzing these interview transcripts, researchers uncovered significant patterns and practices that illustrated the integration of CDL into pedagogical practices. By forging meaningful connections across disciplines and promoting student autonomy, teachers broadened the limits of what can be accomplished in content classrooms. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Transforming Classrooms: A Review on the Importance of Implementing Culturally Responsive Teaching to Address Educational Inequities
text_snippet: Transforming Classrooms: A Review on the Importance of Implementing Culturally Responsive Teaching to Address Educational Inequities The contemporary educational landscape is marked by a significant achievement gap between students of color and their white peers, exacerbated by a standardized testing system. Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT) offers a crucial pedagogical approach to bridge this gap by creating more equitable learning environments. This paper employs a collaborative autoethnography methodology, drawing on the author’s personal and professional experiences to explore CRT’s theoretical and practical aspects. The paper examines the challenges and opportunities associated with implementing CRT through a comprehensive literature review, highlighting its potential to transform educational outcomes for diverse student populations. The findings underscore the importance of understanding and integrating students’ cultural backgrounds to enhance engagement and academic success. This study advances human knowledge by providing actionable strategies for educators to embed CRT within their classrooms, fostering more inclusive and supportive educational environments.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Enacting Culturally Informed Literacy Instruction Within Contexts of Restrictive Policies
text_snippet: Enacting Culturally Informed Literacy Instruction Within Contexts of Restrictive Policies In 2022 our state, like others across the nation, passed legislation restricting the teaching of race and racism (i.e. “divisive concepts”) and in 2023 passed legislation related to the teaching of literacy using evidence-based, science of reading approaches. As an urban institution with a mission to prepare teachers who address social justice and equity, we were concerned about how this political context would impact our graduates’ ability to enact culturally responsive approaches to literacy instruction. Our findings indicate teachers’ efforts centered on texts and instructional approaches reflecting students’ backgrounds, culture, and language expertise. Overall, the school systems move to scripted programs adhering to a Science of Reading approach seemed to result in a more restrictive context for implementing culturally informed instruction than did the divisive concepts law. Teachers’ efforts to be culturally responsive were supported when teachers had the autonomy to make instructional decisions in light of their knowledge of the students. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Dear Reader: Book Banning’s Threat to BIPOC Educators
text_snippet: Dear Reader: Book Banning’s Threat to BIPOC Educators Our educational system has been political and complex since the introduction of public schooling. Additionally, schools and teachers serve multiple purposes, from teaching curricular content to fostering social, emotional, and interpersonal skills in their students. The issue of book banning in schools raises critical questions about who controls students’ access to literature. This form of censorship undermines public trust in educators’ ability to make informed curricular decisions, eroding their capacity to authentically teach important content that helps students develop critical thinking skills in a diverse world. I argue that the book-banning movement is not just an attempt to limit controversial material, but a political agenda aimed at sanitizing and whitewashing K-12 curricula. This agenda threatens to erase both collective and individual histories, turning schools into spaces of manufactured thought rather than liberatory learning environments. The impact of book banning extends beyond limiting access to knowledge; it also harms Black educators. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Welcome to Ms. Bonny’s Class: Searching for Culturally Relevant Practices in My Own Teaching
text_snippet: Welcome to Ms. Bonny’s Class: Searching for Culturally Relevant Practices in My Own Teaching In this autoethnographic study, I examine ways that, if at all, my teaching practices provide my elementary urban-school students with a culturally relevant education. I use Gloria Ladson-Billings’s (1995) culturally relevant education theoretical framework to analyze the written transcriptions of my recorded live teachings. Findings show my strengths as a culturally relevant educator: 1) I push all students to produce high rigor work, 2) I uplift students by giving positive reinforcement while encouraging vulnerability to make mistakes, 3) I scaffold lessons to support the academic development of all students 4) I validate their perspectives and feelings using straightforward feedback and empathy. This research also shows me the aspects that I need to further address in my journey to becoming a culturally relevant educator. Finally, this research illustrates that I need to continue reflecting on my own practices to best support all students so that they become successful in a world language urban classroom, and I must continue working on refining my educational practices to get closer to becoming a culturally relevant educator. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Addressing Teacher Shortages in Urban Schools Through Partnerships
text_snippet: Addressing Teacher Shortages in Urban Schools Through Partnerships Partnerships among professionals within urban school districts and teacher preparation programs are necessary to address teacher shortages through innovative and sustained professional learning from initial clinical experiences through induction (Yendol-Hoppey & Hoppey, 2018). A collaborative model of teacher preparation was envisioned and implemented by faculty and administrators in a large, urban school district to address teacher shortages through continued professional learning, coaching, mentoring, and supports within High Need Schools (HNS). The focus of this manuscript describes an enhanced partnership model and specific programmatic components of a reconceptualized continuum of professional learning and roles by university faculty, supervising teachers, and preservice teachers. Specific impacts from program implementation are shared. Lastly, considerations for enhancement and sustainability of the innovative model are described.

title: Advanced Placement and Black High School Students: A Logistical Regression of College Persistence Factors
text_snippet: Advanced Placement and Black High School Students: A Logistical Regression of College Persistence Factors The purpose of the present study was to examine how Advanced Placement (AP) course participation influences the postsecondary persistence of Black students compared to other commonly examined factors using a nine-predictor logistic regression model. We extracted from the 2012/14 Beginning Postsecondary Students Longitudinal Study (BPS:12/14). Black students represented 13.9 percent (N = 3475) of the BPS:12/14 student sample. Our research focuses on Black students and considers the effect of their intersecting characteristics on persistence in postsecondary settings. The results suggest that AP courses have a statistically significant positive effect on their odds of college persistence (OR = 1.67). Specifically, compared to student GPA (OR=1.68), AP course participation had the largest effect on student persistence in postsecondary education. The present study contributes to the literature by providing group-specific effect size benchmark data to characterize the impact of unique factors on the persistence of Black students in postsecondary education. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Retaining African American Teachers in Urban Settings: A Literature Review of Successful Strategies Utilized by Principals
text_snippet: Retaining African American Teachers in Urban Settings: A Literature Review of Successful Strategies Utilized by Principals School administrators contribute to the macro and micro environmental factors that challenge the sustainability of African American teachers. Retaining African American teachers is a particular challenge for schools that serve high proportions of students of color living in households with low-income. Although some research focuses on the attrition of teachers of color that include, but are not limited to, poor work environments, these conditions are most common in schools that enroll socio-economically disenfranchised students. However, literary reviews point to strategies that can work in such settings and more. Thus, this literature review examines effective strategies used by principals to sustain African American teachers in diverse schools. Critical Learning Theory framed the categories for this research. Critical Learning Theory explains the process for education and racial dignity. The longevity of African American teachers is dependent on the layers of support provided by principals. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Graduation Rates and Math Proficiency in an Urban School District: A Counter-Narrative
text_snippet: Graduation Rates and Math Proficiency in an Urban School District: A Counter-Narrative This article examines high school graduation rates and Algebra I proficiency rates in a large urban school district in Maryland. The article approaches this problem from a critical race theory perspective. The article challenges the school district’s received narrative that it is doing well for its minority students. Using a counter-narrative framework and a critical quantitative approach, the article builds a counter-narrative to the school district’s narrative using the school district’s own high school graduation and Algebra I proficiency data. The data show that African-American and especially Hispanic students are not succeeding to the degree the official narrative suggests. Free and reduced-price meal data are also used to show the strong relationship between low income and racial composition in the high schools in the district. Recommendations for improving Algebra I pedagogy are suggested.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: FROM THE LENS OF MIDDLE SCHOOL STUDENTS: FACTORS THAT PROMOTED THEIR ACADEMIC RESILIENCE
text_snippet: FROM THE LENS OF MIDDLE SCHOOL STUDENTS: FACTORS THAT PROMOTED THEIR ACADEMIC RESILIENCE While much has been studied addressing the topic of academic resilience, few researchers have examined adolescent perceptions of the factors that contribute to school success. This qualitative interpretive study explored individual protective factors that can promote academic resilience in urban middle school students. One-on-one interviews (N = 20) of students living in one urban setting were conducted. After analysis, the four individual protective factors of positive self-esteem, self-determination, perseverance, and optimism were identified. Implications are recommended, such as offering these adolescents the opportunity to voice their experiences to educational leaders, and further research avenues are suggested.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Examining Urban Teachers’ Working Conditions Response to Resilience Following the Results of Covid-19
text_snippet: Examining Urban Teachers’ Working Conditions Response to Resilience Following the Results of Covid-19 There are many rewards associated with teaching in public schools, but there are also several challenges such as understaffing, limited resources, overcrowded classrooms, and underpaid employees. All of these issues combined often lead to burnout and mental health concerns among public school teachers, particularly those in urban settings. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, literature regarding teachers’ psychological distress has increased in a general sense; however, there remains limited exploration of a potential increase in job-related mental health concerns of urban teachers after the onset of COVID. Therefore, in this study we compare the 2018 (pre-COVID), 2020 (early-COVID), and 2022 (during/post-COVID) results of the North Carolina Teacher Working Conditions Survey in order to answer whether there has been a change in the psychological distress of urban school teachers in North Carolina during these time frames. Based on the findings, we offer recommendations to key stakeholders in an effort to better support the health and outcomes of K-12 urban school teachers as they continue adapting to the ever-expanding and ever-evolving implications of COVID.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Da Math Ain’t Mathin’: Evaluating Black Students’ Language Use in Mathematics Education
text_snippet: Da Math Ain’t Mathin’: Evaluating Black Students’ Language Use in Mathematics Education Foundational principles of formal math language in mathematics classrooms are necessary for students’ ability to succeed academically. However, cultural dialects such as Black language are vilified within the scope of education, particularly in mathematics education, despite evidence that using students’ cultural and linguistic backgrounds aids in their understanding of mathematical concepts. In a sociopolitical context that does not support the use of culture as it relates to race and gender, educators face even more challenges in pursuit of linguistic and cultural justice. This article facilitates critical conversations regarding mathematics teaching, learning, and culture and its implications on Black students. To this end, we provide recommendations for stakeholders in mathematics education that can provide a starting point to make mathematics education a more welcoming discipline.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Black Gaze Framework: Centering & Celebrating Blackness in Education for Liberation
text_snippet: Black Gaze Framework: Centering & Celebrating Blackness in Education for Liberation Black Gaze Framework (BGF) is a promising pathway to center and celebrate Blackness in education for liberation. We provide an overview of anti-Blackness within education and teacher education, share the BGF, and apply that framework to courses within teacher education, we have taught. Like BlackCrit, BGF calls for “the specificity of the Black” (Dumas & ross, 2016) and moves into action to center Blackness for liberation in education. BGF has five tenets: Honoring the O.G.’s: Black History & Wisdom; Elevating Our Stories: Black Multifaceted Experiences; Preaching Points: Action Steps for Black Folx; What You Reading, Though?: Black Thought Past & Present; and I See You!: Black Acknowledgement & Elevation.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Narratives of Disability and the Other Latino: Stories of Diversity and Inclusion in a Teacher Preparation Program at an Urban University
text_snippet: Narratives of Disability and the Other Latino: Stories of Diversity and Inclusion in a Teacher Preparation Program at an Urban University This self-reflective article describes my experience as a disabled-Latino faculty member in a teacher preparation program at a minority-serving urban university. This personal narrative of the physical, emotional, attitudinal, and resource aspects of the author’s experience highlights barriers and challenges experienced in the educational and working environment while identifying strategies that assisted in overcoming these barriers. The article specifically relates my progression through my teaching career as I encounter issues of equality and diversity. With this article, disabled faculty and other minority groups are encouraged to incorporate practices that encourage teacher candidates to explore teaching practices for diverse populations in urban settings.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Instructional Practices of High School English Language Teachers in Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Classrooms: A Case Study
text_snippet: Instructional Practices of High School English Language Teachers in Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Classrooms: A Case Study Grounded within the tenets of culturally responsive education, this qualitative case study examined the culturally responsive instructional practices of teachers working with linguistically, ethnically, and culturally diverse students in sheltered English Language Arts (ELA) classrooms that mainly serve English language learners in an urban high school located in the Midwest United States. Three teachers participated in the study through interviews and observations. The findings of the study indicate that the inclusion of culturally and linguistically affirming and familiar tasks, including translanguaging, led to greater student engagement and academic gains in the sheltered ELA classroom.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Black Women Principals and Expressions of Culturally Responsive School Leadership During Crisis: An Exploratory Study
text_snippet: Black Women Principals and Expressions of Culturally Responsive School Leadership During Crisis: An Exploratory Study Schools experience a plethora of crises from pandemics, school shootings, weather-related traumas, and mass migrations that require school leaders to create solutions to support students and their families. Researchers have explored school leaders’ responses to crises but have yet to explore how principals generally and Black women specifically conceptualize and use culturally responsive school leadership (CRSL) practices as a part of their response. In this qualitative study we explored how 9 Black women school leaders implemented CRSL practices when responding to crisis. We found that principals primarily relied upon three domains of CRSL (critical reflection, promoting an inclusive environment, and community engagement) to navigate a crisis and expand opportunities for equity and inclusion¬––even in the face of district opposition. We also found evidence that principals engaged in instructional leadership regardless of the crisis they faced. We provide implications and recommendations for school leaders, K-12 school districts, and administrator preparation programs on how to support leaders responding to crisis.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: The Students Are Hungry: A Conceptual Model to Understanding Food Insecurity Among Minoritized College Students at Urban Higher Education Institutions
text_snippet: The Students Are Hungry: A Conceptual Model to Understanding Food Insecurity Among Minoritized College Students at Urban Higher Education Institutions Approximately one in five college students suffers from food insecurity, however, racially/ethnically minoritized students attending urban universities are more likely to experience food insecurity. Although these concerns are well documented, there has been a gap in the theory-driven tools used by higher education professionals to alleviate food insecurity for minoritized students at urban institutions. Guided by a reconceptualized Ecological Systems Model (Network-Ecological Systems Model), this present study aims to identify a model and solutions on food insecurity mitigation for minoritized college students in urban institutions. Findings of the developed model suggest pathways of social connections that higher education professionals can use for direct alleviation of food insecurity, which has major implications for the academic achievement, social connections, and a general sense of belonging and belonging.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Stepping Out and Stepping Up: Narratives of Women of Color in an Urban STEM OST Program
text_snippet: Stepping Out and Stepping Up: Narratives of Women of Color in an Urban STEM OST Program The science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields have a well-documented racialized and gendered participation gap between males, particularly white males, and women of color (WOC). Through a Critical Race Feminist lens, this qualitative research study uses life-story narrative analysis to understand the experiences of eleven WOC who participated in an urban STEM-focused out-of-school time (OST) program. Data analysis showed students story their experiences around three overarching themes: (1) Experiencing New Opportunities; (2) Cultivating Supportive Relationships; and (3) Expanding STEM Career Possibilities. Findings indicate that an urban STEM-focused OST program can activate an ecosystem of opportunities and support which can empower WOC to step out of their socialized comfort zones and step up to more advanced academic and career paths. Participant narratives demonstrate how their experiences in a particular urban STEM OST program opened doors and encouraged pathways otherwise historically made inaccessible to WOC in STEM fields.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Illuminating Effective Practices, Approaches, and Strategies in Urban Education
text_snippet: Illuminating Effective Practices, Approaches, and Strategies in Urban Education Just as horticulturalists shift, change, and alter the growing environment for their potential harvest as necessary, if urban educators and scholars want to change the outcomes urban students experience, we must change the soil in which urban students grow. Simply put, in the words of Alexander Den Heijer (n.d.), “when a flower doesn’t bloom, you fix the environment in which it grows, not the flower.” If always focused on the flower (student achievement/discipline outcomes), the analysis rests on what grows instead of the environment in which it grows and will continue to miss opportunities to revitalize the soil of urban environments.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Examining Discipline Integrity Among Black Girls in Urban Schools
text_snippet: Examining Discipline Integrity Among Black Girls in Urban Schools The subject of school discipline and its related disparities and controversies has been of primary interest in education over the past six decades (Children’s Defense Fund, 1975; Green, 2022, Skiba et al., 2002; Staats, 2014). Many of the interests have been largely centered on topics concerning the criminalization, victimization and exclusion of students of color (Crenshaw, 2015; Lewis et al., 2010), disproportionate discipline sanctions (Blake et al., 2011) and intersectional violence (Annamma et al., 2019). Although much has been documented about the topic, less has been written about strength-based, equity-focused approaches and solutions that (1) support the sustainability of Black girls and educators and (2) inspire educational stakeholders towards cultivating cultures of care in schools through policy and practice. Exploring approaches such as discipline integrity can help address the discipline and well-being concerns specific to Black girls in urban schools.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: The Tale of Two Cities: A Critical Spatial Analysis of Access to Two-Way Dual Language Programs in San Antonio and Austin
text_snippet: The Tale of Two Cities: A Critical Spatial Analysis of Access to Two-Way Dual Language Programs in San Antonio and Austin Texas is home to a burgeoning linguistically diverse population, which has contributed to the exponential growth of bilingual education programming across the state. One program type, two-way dual language (TWDL), has become a popular enrichment model of bilingual education and has received increased attention and funding at the state level. While bilingual education was originally intended to serve linguistically diverse, primarily Latinx, students, there is a growing body of research that suggests the rapid growth of TWDL has come to serve primarily white, affluent, English-dominant students. The present study sought to contribute to this research by examining the locations of TWDL within two major cities in Texas: San Antonio and Austin. This tale of two cities employed a critical race spatial analysis to describe TWDL locational patterns within San Antonio and Austin based on neighborhood demographics including race/ethnicity and socioeconomics. Findings suggest that access to TWDL in each city is based on differing factors, with the socio-historical contexts of San Antonio and Austin playing a major role in the accessibility of TWDL today. journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Current and Future Trends in Urban Areas: Strategies for Transforming Learning, Teaching and Research - AERA SIG Keynote
text_snippet: Current and Future Trends in Urban Areas: Strategies for Transforming Learning, Teaching and Research - AERA SIG Keynote This publication is an excerpt from my keynote address to the Urban Learning, Teaching and Research Special Interest Group at the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting in Chicago, IL at the request of the incoming Chair. This excerpt, while brief, overviews some key trends that the membership needs to consider as they consider the future of their scholarly work. A few trends highlighted during the keynote address are provided along with key questions for the membership to consider in the future.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: The Importance of Culturally Relevant Pedagogy in the Era of COVID: Using Documentary Film to Tell Stories from the Front Line
text_snippet: The Importance of Culturally Relevant Pedagogy in the Era of COVID: Using Documentary Film to Tell Stories from the Front Line The COVID-19 global pandemic forced teachers and schools to rethink everything about the educational process. They were left in their own homes to face the challenges of binary pandemics: healthcare and racial injustice, and the need for Culturally Relevant Pedagogy became as important as ever. This article provides a view into the lives of teachers in urban schools who relied on the tenets of Culturally Relevant Pedagogy to serve their students. Twenty-five teachers were interviewed for a documentary film and several themes emerged, including resiliency, empathy, professional respect, and social justice activism.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: Exploring How a Hip-Hop Based Science Program Afforded Black/Brown Girls the Space to Resist Against Black/Brown Negative Stereotypes in STEM
text_snippet: Exploring How a Hip-Hop Based Science Program Afforded Black/Brown Girls the Space to Resist Against Black/Brown Negative Stereotypes in STEM This longitudinal critical ethnographic study gave voices to Black and Brown girls who are racially and traditionally marginalized in STEM education. With the understanding that current science curricula are not culturally inclusive (Adjapong & Emdin, 2015; Atwater, 1996; Emdin, 2016; Ladson-Billings, 1995; Mensah, 2012; Takaki, 2012), the researchers explored the girls’ responses to a science program that focused on addressing some of the existing cultural divides between urban youth of color and their counterparts, namely the Science Genius program. The goal of the study was to find out if the confidence and the engagement level of Black and Brown girls changed, and to what extent negative societal stereotypes about Black and Brown girls in science could be addressed if science were culturally relevant to their daily lives. We argue that the results of the study will provide insight into how to increase the diverse pool of participants into STEM career fields.

journal_name: Journal of Urban Learning, Teaching, and Research
title: “Can We Call this Racism?” YES! Disrupting White Educational Spaces and Affirming Students’ Positive “Possible Selves”
text_snippet: “Can We Call this Racism?” YES! Disrupting White Educational Spaces and Affirming Students’ Positive “Possible Selves” As two White, privileged educators and researchers, we have questioned, challenged, and examined how to best operate in diverse classrooms, keeping in mind our joint goals of advancing socially just teaching agendas alongside our desire not to “whitesplain” issues centering on race to students of color. Through narrative case phenomenology and Critical Whiteness Studies frameworks, we analyze separate classroom events in which racialized content was both unexpected and foregrounded. Our responses in these moments, and our ensuing conversations and intellectual discussions, serve as data for this paper. Additionally, these scenarios are ripe for analysis as we have served either as teachers or researchers with distinct priorities and roles. The classroom scenarios we present have caused both our personal introspection and professional growth. Implications for practice include our assessment of anti-racist teaching as a moral and ethical issue that belongs in classroom space, no matter the educational circumstances.

title: Reading and Mathematics Elementary School Performance of Spanish-speaking Children Matriculating from a Bilingual Preschool
text_snippet: Reading and Mathematics Elementary School Performance of Spanish-speaking Children Matriculating from a Bilingual Preschool The Charlotte Bilingual Preschool (CltBP), situated in the 17th largest urban area of the US, has found itself at the intersection of its community’s agendas to provide high quality preschool services to Spanish-speaking families, improve opportunities for upward mobility, and foster literacy gains for children from birth through third grade. This study seeks to determine if the preschool’s bilingual approach has any impact on its alumni students’ reading and mathematics performance in kindergarten, first, and second grade. DIBELS and MAP testing, as well as standards-based grades, were compared between CltBP alumni and their identified Hispanic peers within the public school system. Findings show that CltBP alumni not only score ahead of their peers in reading and mathematics upon entering public school kindergarten, this advantage continues through second grade. Despite this advantage, many CltBP alumni still continue to perform below state-identified proficiency levels.

title: Evidence Based Funding in Illinois: A Discussion of Equity in Urban Education
text_snippet: Evidence Based Funding in Illinois: A Discussion of Equity in Urban Education In this pilot study, we examine the realities of differential funding structures across the US, which disproportionately disadvantage historically marginalized communities (Black and Brown students) and students living in poverty, contributing to an intractable opportunity gap. Prior research indicates that equitable funding can, in fact, decrease the opportunity gap between dominant and non-dominant-culture students. We use the new funding structure in Illinois as a case study in funding equity that should be applied nationally. We critique the current funding structure of public schools in general, which has defamed the public sector in favor of school choice, vouchers, and charter schools—all with less oversight than public schools and structured to profit from public monies. Finally, we address the impact of COVID-19 on existing funding inequities.

title: AMP Centers: A Case Study of the Intersection of Critical Urban Education and Action Research
text_snippet: AMP Centers: A Case Study of the Intersection of Critical Urban Education and Action Research The Action Mapping Project (AMP) is a youth-oriented participatory action project that conducts research and education programs in high schools and middle schools in Tacoma, Washington. AMP uses participatory community mapping to generate new forms of data and conducts educational programs with high school students that center on the use of GIS (geographic information systems) to analyze data and produce maps of local knowledge to influence public policy in underserved neighborhoods. In this article, AMP’s educational program (AMP Centers) is used as a case study of how principles of action research and critical education can be placed into practice.
